svg.text: A PHILOSOPHY OF SOFTWARE DESIGN · JOHN OUSTERHOUT

text.tspan: than it shows, so the people…

svg.text: The best modules give a lot of power through a small,
simple interface. Think of each module as a rectangle:
its area is what it does, its top edge is what it asks.
A deep module hides far more than it shows, so the
people who call it learn little and get a great deal.
Shallow modules are the opposite: an interface nearly
as complex as the work behind it, so it costs more
than it saves. Design the interface around its use:
the common case should be the simplest thing to call.
The Unix file calls are the classic example of a
deep interface: five calls hide hundreds of thousands

text.tspan: of lines of disk management, caching and scheduling.

svg.text: Length by itself is rarely the problem; what matters
is whether the method hides something worth hiding.
A class whose methods only pass their arguments on
to another class adds an interface and hides nothing.
Counted on the original Unix interface; later kernels
add calls, but the shape of the interface holds.
A deep module hides far more than it
shows, so the people who call it…

Select words: four colours that mean something — Idea, Question, Quote, To discuss — and Add a note.
The passage takes the colour at once; keys 1–4 pick one, N adds a note, Esc cancels and the mark goes.
On a wide pane the margin lists the chapter's highlights in reading order, each with its colour as
a bar; the chips filter by colour. Open the notebook shows everything you marked in the book.
Click a footnote mark: the note floats over the page, Go to note jumps to it. Your reading line
stays marked, so closing it (Esc) leaves you exactly where you were.
After a link inside the book, a pill says where you came from: one press, or Esc, back to p. 84.
Ctrl+F searches the whole book in a slim bar under the header: 12 results, Enter and ↑ ↓ step through.
Each result shows its snippet, chapter and page. The current match is outlined in the text, the
others are tinted, and the panel closes with the bar.
Time left, quietly: only while the bar shows (the pointer moves or a key is pressed), then it fades
with it. Never a number that sits on the page while you read.
On a phone the popover sits under the selection: four round swatches, then Add a note and Copy.
